subject: Economy
sub_topic: Types of economies — market, command, mixed

concepts.name: Price Mechanism in Market Economy: Allocation and Signaling
key_dimensions: How prices signal resource scarcity and guide production decisions without central authority
Role of supply-demand equilibrium vs. government-set prices — UPSC trap: MSP/MRP in India as partial price controls within a mixed economy
Invisible hand concept (Adam Smith) and its limitations in public goods and externalities
Comparison with command economy where prices are administratively determined

concepts.name: Command Economy: Central Planning Mechanism and Soviet Model
key_dimensions: Five-Year Plans as the instrument of command economy — distinction between Soviet Five-Year Plans and India's Five-Year Plans (UPSC trap: India's plans were indicative, not mandatory)
Role of central planning authority (e.g., Gosplan in USSR) vs. NITI Aayog in India
Soft budget constraint problem and inefficiency in state-owned enterprises
Why command economies collapsed — information asymmetry (Hayek's knowledge problem)

concepts.name: Mixed Economy: Definition, Spectrum, and India's Model
key_dimensions: Mixed economy is not a fixed point but a spectrum — degree of state vs. market varies (UPSC trap: assuming all mixed economies are identical)
India's mixed economy framework: public sector in commanding heights vs. private sector in consumer goods
Industrial Policy Resolution 1948 and 1956 as constitutional/legal basis for India's mixed economy structure
Post-1991 shift: India's mixed economy tilting toward market — LPG reforms significance

concepts.name: Public Goods vs. Private Goods: Market Failure Justification
key_dimensions: Non-excludability and non-rivalry as defining characteristics — UPSC trap: quasi-public goods (toll roads, cable TV) classified correctly
Free-rider problem as the core reason markets underprovide public goods
Role of government provision of public goods as the economic rationale for a mixed/command element
Examples: National defense, lighthouse (pure public goods) vs. common pool resources (rival but non-excludable) — four-quadrant classification

concepts.name: Market Failures: Types and Policy Responses
key_dimensions: Four types: public goods, externalities, information asymmetry, monopoly power — UPSC trap: confusing market failure with government failure
Externalities (positive/negative) as justification for taxes (Pigouvian tax) and subsidies
Information asymmetry: Adverse selection vs. moral hazard — examples in insurance, credit markets (relevant to financial inclusion)
Natural monopoly as a special case — why utilities are regulated or state-owned in mixed economies

concepts.name: Opportunity Cost: The Core Concept Behind Economic Decisions
key_dimensions: Definition: Value of the next best alternative foregone — not just monetary cost
Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) as the graphical representation of opportunity cost and resource constraints
UPSC trap: Opportunity cost of holding foreign exchange reserves, opportunity cost of food subsidy vs. investment
Comparative advantage in trade theory is built on opportunity cost — link to international trade questions

concepts.name: Production Possibility Frontier (PPF): Assumptions, Shifts, and Policy Implications
key_dimensions: Movement along PPF (resource reallocation) vs. outward shift (economic growth via technology/capital) — UPSC trap: confusing the two
Operating inside PPF implies unemployment or inefficiency — relevant to disguised unemployment in agriculture
PPF shape (concave) explains increasing opportunity cost — why specialization has limits
PPF and guns-vs-butter trade-off: defense expenditure vs. social spending in budget analysis

concepts.name: Factors of Production and Their Returns: Land, Labour, Capital, Enterprise
key_dimensions: Returns: Rent (land), Wages (labour), Interest (capital), Profit (enterprise) — UPSC trap: 'interest' on capital is return, not just bank interest
Human capital as a form of capital — distinction from physical capital and relevance to HDI
Factor mobility: differences between market, mixed, and command economies in factor allocation
Disguised unemployment as a labour market concept unique to agrarian mixed economies like India

concepts.name: Role of the State in Economy: Allocative, Distributive, and Stabilization Functions
key_dimensions: Musgrave's three functions of government — UPSC trap: stabilization function (fiscal/monetary policy) is often missed as a state economic role
Allocative function: correcting market failures; Distributive function: reducing inequality via taxes and transfers
Command economy: state dominates all three; Market economy: state minimal; Mixed: selective intervention
DPSP (Article 39) as constitutional mandate for distributive role of Indian state — legal angle

concepts.name: Socialism vs. Capitalism: Ideological Basis and Economic Outcomes
key_dimensions: Socialism: collective ownership and production for use; Capitalism: private ownership and production for profit
UPSC trap: 'Socialist' in Indian Preamble (added 1976) does not mean command economy — India is a democratic socialist mixed economy
Nordic Model as a capitalist-market economy with strong social welfare — not a command economy
Gini coefficient outcomes: command economies claimed equality but often had hidden inequalities (nomenklatura privilege)

concepts.name: Privatization, Nationalization, and Disinvestment: Instruments of Economic System Choice
key_dimensions: Nationalization: state takeover of private assets — India's bank nationalization 1969 as shift toward command elements
Privatization vs. disinvestment: UPSC trap — disinvestment is not always privatization (government may retain majority stake)
Strategic vs. non-strategic disinvestment: Strategic disinvestment involves transfer of management control
NITI Aayog's role in identifying CPSEs for strategic disinvestment — institutional angle

concepts.name: Commanding Heights of the Economy: Concept and India's Evolution
key_dimensions: Term coined by Lenin — refers to key industries (steel, energy, banking) state must control to steer the economy
India's Industrial Policy Resolution 1956: Schedule A (exclusive state domain), Schedule B (mixed), Schedule C (private) — UPSC trap: knowing which industries were in which schedule
Post-1991 dismantling of commanding heights doctrine — only atomic energy, railways retained as state monopoly
Comparison: USSR maintained commanding heights rigidly; India selectively retained them — key difference

concepts.name: Indicative Planning vs. Imperative Planning
key_dimensions: Imperative/directive planning (command economy): targets are mandatory, enforced by state authority
Indicative planning (mixed/market economy): targets are advisory, market incentives used to achieve goals — India's model
UPSC trap: India's Five-Year Plans were indicative for private sector but somewhat directive for public sector undertakings
France's 'dirigisme' as a non-Soviet example of indicative planning in a market economy

concepts.name: Market Economy Institutions: Property Rights, Rule of Law, and Contract Enforcement
key_dimensions: Property rights (Coase theorem) as the foundation of market economy — without clear rights, markets fail
Rule of law and contract enforcement as prerequisites for market efficiency — World Bank Ease of Doing Business indicators
UPSC trap: land titling issues in India as a property rights problem preventing efficient market allocation
Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) as an extension of property rights — TRIPS agreement and India's pharmaceutical industry conflict

concepts.name: Subsidies and Price Controls: Distortions in Mixed Economy
key_dimensions: Price ceiling (below equilibrium): causes shortage — example: rent control, essential commodity price caps
Price floor (above equilibrium): causes surplus — example: MSP leading to grain mountain in FCI godowns
UPSC trap: MSP is a price floor but it only creates surplus if procurement is guaranteed — without procurement, MSP is ineffective
Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) as a move from price distortion to income support — subsidy reform rationale

concepts.name: Externalities and the Polluter-Pays Principle in Mixed Economies
key_dimensions: Negative externality: social cost > private cost — market overproduces (e.g., industrial pollution)
Positive externality: social benefit > private benefit — market underproduces (e.g., education, vaccination)
Pigouvian tax/subsidy as the corrective instrument — carbon tax as a current policy application
UPSC trap: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) under Plastic Waste Rules is an application of polluter-pays in India's mixed economy framework

concepts.name: Consumer Sovereignty in Market Economy vs. Planner Sovereignty in Command Economy
key_dimensions: Consumer sovereignty: what gets produced is determined by consumer preferences expressed through prices
Planner sovereignty: central authority decides what, how, and for whom to produce — three fundamental economic questions
UPSC trap: even in market economies, consumer sovereignty is limited by advertising, monopoly, and information asymmetry
India's shift from planner-determined industrial licensing to market-responsive production post-1991 — practical example

concepts.name: Gig Economy and Platform Economy: New Variants Challenging Traditional Classifications
key_dimensions: Gig economy blurs the line between employee and entrepreneur — challenges classical factor-of-production classification
Platform economies (Uber, Amazon) create two-sided markets — not purely market or mixed, raises new regulatory questions
UPSC trap: Gig workers lack social security — Code on Social Security 2020 attempts to bring them under mixed-economy welfare net
Network effects in platform economy lead to natural monopoly tendencies — market failure in a 'market economy' context

concepts.name: Washington Consensus vs. Post-Washington Consensus: Ideological Shift in Development Economics
key_dimensions: Washington Consensus (1989): 10 prescriptions including privatization, deregulation, fiscal discipline — neoliberal push toward market economy
Post-Washington Consensus: acknowledged market failures, emphasized institutions, governance, social safety nets — mixed economy rehabilitation
UPSC trap: IMF's SAP (Structural Adjustment Programs) forced command/mixed economies toward market — India's 1991 reforms partly influenced by this
Stiglitz's critique of Washington Consensus — premature financial liberalization causes crises (East Asian crisis 1997 example)

concepts.name: Transition Economies: Moving from Command to Market — Challenges and Lessons
key_dimensions: Shock therapy (rapid privatization — Poland, Russia) vs. gradualism (China, Vietnam) — two transition strategies
UPSC trap: China is still classified as a command/socialist market economy — not a pure market economy despite market mechanisms
Oligarchy problem in Russia's transition: rapid privatization without institutions led to asset stripping, not efficiency
India's 1991 reforms as a partial transition — not shock therapy, but managed liberalization with retained public sector role
